mainTopic: When a lender takes land back from a buyer (טורף מן הלקוחות), who gets the שבח (improvement) the buyer added? The גמרא works to fit שמואל's ruling with a ברייתא that seems to disagree.
overview: This amud begins by finishing an answer about a lender who takes land back from a buyer who improved it. Is the lender allowed to keep the buyer's שבח? The גמרא first fits שמואל together with a ברייתא by looking at how ripe the produce is. When that fails, it splits them by the size of the debt, and it closes with the case of an אפותיקי. Next comes a new dispute about a buyer who knew the field was stolen. רב says he gets his money back because it was a פקדון. שמואל says he does not, because it was a מתנה. The גמרא shows that the same dispute appears with a man who does קידושין with his sister, and explains why both cases are needed. רבא then rules like רב, and he also rules that a missing אחריות clause is a טעות סופר. Finally, שמואל asks רב about a גזלן who sold a field and later bought it from the real owner. The amud ends partway through explaining the practical difference between מר זוטרא and רב אשי, and that explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Ripe produce versus unripe produce
steps.stepSummary: The end of an answer begun on the previous page. The ברייתא (lender pays for שבח) is about produce that 'reaches the shoulders.' שמואל (lender collects the שבח) is about produce that does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: [There, the ברייתא is talking about improvement] that reaches the shoulders. Here, שמואל is talking about improvement that does not reach the shoulders.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to the contradiction between שמואל and the ברייתא. It splits them into two different kinds of crops.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Produce that is almost ready to harvest and carry on your shoulders counts as separate from the land. So the lender cannot just take it; he must pay the buyer for it. Produce that is still growing counts as part of the land, so the lender collects it along with the field.

keyTerms.meaning: Improvement or added value the buyer brought to the land
'Reaches the shoulders': produce almost ready to harvest and carry away
Here: pointing to the second of the two sources being contrasted

phrases.english: that reaches the shoulders;
phrases.notes: This is the end of an answer that started on the previous page: 'There (in the ברייתא) it means improvement...'

phrases.english: here, it is improvement that does not reach the shoulders.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer from the previous page to the contradiction between שמואל and the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source is talking about a different stage of produce.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל and the ברייתא seem to disagree directly about who gets the שבח.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about ripe produce (lender pays). שמואל is about unripe produce (lender collects it with the land).

steps.title: שמואל ruled every day even on ripe produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the answer. In real cases that happened all the time, שמואל let lenders collect even ripe produce without paying.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there are cases every single day, and שמואל has the lender collect even improvement that reaches the shoulders!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. It points to שמואל's actual rulings in court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last answer said שמואל only gave the lender unripe produce. But שמואל's everyday practice shows he gave the lender even ripe produce. So the 'ripe versus unripe' split cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: Real cases that happen every day: proof from actual practice
Has someone collect payment (the court lets the lender collect)

phrases.english: But there are incidents every day,
and שמואל has the lender collect
even improvement that reaches the shoulders!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the ripe/unripe distinction from step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that שמואל only applies to unripe produce.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל's actual daily rulings gave lenders even ripe produce, so his rule cannot be limited to unripe produce.

steps.title: It depends on how big the debt is
steps.stepSummary: A new answer. When the debt equals the land plus the שבח, the lender takes everything (שמואל). When the debt equals only the land, the lender pays the buyer for the שבח (the ברייתא).
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. In this case, the lender is owed as much as the land plus the improvement. In that case, he is owed only as much as the land. There, the lender gives the buyer the value of his improvement and sends him away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new way to fit שמואל and the ברייתא together. This time the split is based on the size of the debt, not the ripeness of the crop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the debt is big enough to cover the land and the שבח, the lender may take all of it, even ripe produce. That explains שמואל's daily cases. If the debt covers only the land, the lender has no claim to the extra value, so he pays the buyer for the שבח and takes the field.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is not difficult': opens an answer that splits two cases
He is owed by him (the lender has a debt claim against the borrower)
He removes him: pays him off and ends his claim

steps.whatToRemember: In this answer, the lender collects the שבח only up to the size of his debt. If the debt covers only the land, he must pay the buyer for the שבח.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is where he is owed by him
the amount of the land and the improvement.
That is where he is owed by him
only the amount of the land,
so he gives him his improvement
and removes him.
phrases.notes: The lender pays the buyer for the improvement, and then the buyer has to leave the field.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דְּמַסֵּיק בֵּיהּ כְּשִׁיעוּר אַרְעָא וּשְׁבָחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 2 with a new distinction that replaces the one in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the size of the debt.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ripeness could not explain the difference, so שמואל and the ברייתא seemed to clash again.
steps.terutzMaskana: Debt = land + שבח: the lender takes all (שמואל). Debt = land only: the lender pays for the שבח (the ברייתא).

steps.title: The buyer should get a piece of land worth his improvement
steps.stepSummary: This answer works only for the view that a buyer cannot pay off the lender with money. According to the view that he can, the buyer should be able to say: 'Since I have no cash, give me a piece of this land equal to my שבח.'
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says that even if the buyer has money, he cannot pay off the lender. But according to the one who says that when the buyer has money he can pay off the lender, let the buyer say to him: 'If I had money, I would have paid you off from the whole field. Now that I have no money, give me a portion of this land equal to my improvement!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 3. It uses a disagreement about whether a buyer can pay the lender cash instead of losing the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two views. One says a buyer must hand over the land and cannot pay cash. The other says a buyer with money may pay the lender and keep the land. Under the second view, the buyer has some right to choose how the lender is paid. So he should be able to keep a piece of land worth his שבח instead of taking money for it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This works well for the one who says': sets up a challenge from the opposite view
The buyer who bought the field from the borrower
The lender (creditor)
Money (literally, זוזים coins)
A measure of land (about a סאה's worth of planting area)

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge works only according to the view that a buyer may pay the lender in cash. It does not apply according to the view that a buyer must give up the land.

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says:
if the buyer has money,

phrases.aramaic: לָא מָצֵי מְסַלֵּיק לֵיהּ לְבַעַל חוֹב, שַׁפִּיר.
phrases.english: he cannot pay off the lender: that is fine.
But according to the one who says
when the buyer has money
he can pay off the lender,
let him say to him:
'If I had money,
I would have paid you off from the whole land.
Now that I have no money,
give me a portion of land
phrases.notes: גריבא is a measure of land, about the area you would plant with a סאה of seed.

phrases.english: in this land
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'in land'; the words in square brackets are the corrected wording, 'in this land,' meaning the very field being taken.

phrases.english: equal to my improvement!'

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר: אִי אִית לֵיהּ זוּזֵי לְלוֹקֵחַ לָא מָצֵי מְסַלֵּיק לֵיהּ לְבַעַל חוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 3's ruling that the lender simply pays the buyer for the שבח.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in step 3 that, when the debt covers only the land, the lender pays money for the שבח and takes the whole field.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a buyer with money may pay off the lender and keep the land, then a buyer without money should at least be able to keep a piece of land worth his שבח, instead of being forced to take cash.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the answer in step 3 depends on which side of the dispute you hold: whether a buyer can pay off the lender with money.

steps.title: The field was set aside as the only source of payment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the question from Step 4. The case is one where the borrower made the field an אפותיקי, so the lender is paid only from this field.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here we are dealing with a case where the borrower made the field an אפותיקי. He told the lender: 'You will be paid only from this field.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 4. It says the case is a special one: the field was set aside as the lender's only source of payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 4 the buyer wanted to say, 'Give me a piece of land equal to my שבח.' That request fails when the borrower promised the lender, 'you will be paid only from this field.' The whole field is tied to the lender, so the buyer cannot take any part of it away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Here, what are we dealing with?' This phrase introduces a narrower case that solves a problem.
A field the borrower sets aside as the special and only source for paying back a debt.
Repayment of a debt.

steps.whatToRemember: The answer that splits the case by how much the debt is worth holds up. The buyer cannot take back a piece of the land because the field was an אפותיקי, set aside only for this lender.

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
A case where he made it an apoteiki,
phrases.notes: The borrower, who later sold the field, had set it aside for the lender.

phrases.english: for he said to him:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יְהֵא לְךָ פֵּרָעוֹן אֶלָּא מִזּוֹ.
phrases.english: You will have no repayment except from this one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 4 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer could ask for a piece of land equal to his שבח.
steps.terutzMaskana: Not when the field was an אפותיקי. The lender is owed this whole field.

steps.title: Buying a field you know is stolen: רב and שמואל disagree
steps.stepSummary: A new case: someone buys a field knowing it does not belong to the seller. רב says the buyer gets his money back but not his שבח. שמואל says he does not even get his money back.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a buyer knew the field was not the seller's and bought it anyway, then when the owner takes it back: רב says the buyer gets his money back but not his improvements. שמואל says he does not even get his money back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic. It brings a disagreement between רב and שמואל about a buyer who knowingly bought a stolen field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the buyer did not know there was a problem with the field. Here he knew from the start that the seller was not the real owner. Both רב and שמואל agree that he loses his שבח. They argue about whether he can get back the price he paid.

keyTerms.meaning: He knew the field did not belong to the seller.
Money. Here it means the price the buyer paid.
The improvement or increase in value of the field.

phrases.english: If he recognized that it was not his
phrases.notes: 'His' means the seller's. The buyer knew the field was stolen and the real owner later takes it back.

phrases.english: and he bought it anyway,
Rav says:
he gets back his money,
he does not get the improvement.
And Shmuel says:
he does not even get back his money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about a buyer who knew the field was stolen.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the buyer gets his money back but not his שבח. שמואל: he does not even get his money back.

steps.title: What is the reason behind their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what idea רב and שמואל disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reasoning behind the disagreement. This line sets up the next steps, where each view is explained.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants to know how each אמורא understands the buyer's payment. Why would the money come back according to רב but not according to שמואל?

keyTerms.meaning: 'About what do they disagree?' This asks for the root idea behind a dispute.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the dispute in Step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason each side gives for its ruling.

steps.title: רב: the money was a deposit
steps.stepSummary: רב holds that the buyer knew he would not end up with the land, so he gave the money as a deposit. A deposit gets returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב holds: a person knows he will not get the land, so he decided to give the money as a deposit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רב's view. The buyer's payment was really a deposit, so he gets it back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer knew the sale would not work. So the money was never really a price for the land. רב says the buyer meant for the seller to hold it for him, which is why he can get it back.

keyTerms.meaning: He made up his mind and gave.
As a deposit, money left with someone to hold and give back.

phrases.english: Rav holds:
a person knows that he has no land,
phrases.notes: He means: the buyer knows he will not get to keep this land.

phrases.english: and he decided and gave it as a deposit.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב סָבַר: אָדָם יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁקַּרְקַע אֵין לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 7 for רב.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The money was meant as a deposit, so it must be returned.

steps.title: Then why not just call it a deposit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if he meant a deposit, he should have said so openly.
steps.simpleTranslation: So let him tell the seller that it is a deposit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's explanation. If the buyer wanted a deposit, why did he pretend to buy the land?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the payment was really a deposit, the buyer could have just said so. Dressing it up as a purchase does not fit what he supposedly wanted.

keyTerms.meaning: 'So let him say to him!' This is a challenge asking why he didn't say it outright.

phrases.english: So let him tell him it is a deposit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's reasoning from Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the money was a deposit.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who wants to give a deposit would simply say so. He would not pretend to buy something.

steps.title: The seller would have refused a deposit
steps.stepSummary: The buyer thought the seller would not agree to hold a deposit, so he presented the money as a purchase.
steps.simpleTranslation: He thought the seller would not accept it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The buyer was afraid the seller would refuse to hold the money as a deposit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding a deposit is a responsibility, and the seller might not want it. So the buyer used the 'sale' as a way to get the seller to hold his money anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: He would not accept.

phrases.english: He thought he would not accept it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: There is no reason to hide a deposit as a sale.
steps.terutzMaskana: He hid it because the seller would have refused to hold a deposit.

steps.title: שמואל: the money was a gift
steps.stepSummary: שמואל holds that the buyer knew he would not end up with the land, so he gave the money as a gift. A gift does not get returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל holds: a person knows he will not get the land, so he decided to give the money as a gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains שמואל's view. The buyer's payment was really a gift, so he cannot get it back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב and שמואל start from the same point: the buyer knew he would not get the land. The only difference is what they think he meant by paying. רב says a deposit, which gets returned. שמואל says a gift, which does not.

keyTerms.meaning: As a gift.

phrases.english: And Shmuel holds:
a person knows that he has no land,
and he decided and gave it as a gift.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל סָבַר: אָדָם יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁקַּרְקַע אֵין לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 7 for שמואל, side by side with רב's view.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The money was meant as a gift, so it is not returned.

steps.title: Then why not just call it a gift?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if he meant a gift, he should have said so openly.
steps.simpleTranslation: So let him tell the seller that it is a gift!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's explanation in the same way it challenged רב's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question is built just like the one in Step 9. If the buyer wanted to give a gift, why pretend it was a purchase?

keyTerms.meaning: A gift.

phrases.english: So let him tell him it is a gift!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's reasoning from Step 11, matching Step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's claim that the money was a gift.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who wants to give a gift would simply say so. He would not pretend to buy something.

steps.title: An open gift would embarrass the seller
steps.stepSummary: Calling it a gift openly would embarrass the seller, so the buyer presented it as a purchase.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter would be embarrassing for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Calling the money a gift would have shamed the seller, so the buyer gave it quietly by calling it a sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking a gift openly can feel like taking charity. The 'sale' let the seller save face while the buyer still meant it as a gift. That is why, according to שמואל, the money is not returned.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter is embarrassing for him.

steps.whatToRemember: רב: the buyer knowingly paid as a deposit, which the seller would not have agreed to hold openly, so he gets his money back. שמואל: he paid as a gift, which would have been embarrassing to give openly, so he does not get his money back. Both agree he does not get his שבח.

phrases.english: The matter is embarrassing for him.
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the seller, who would feel ashamed to be handed an open gift.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: There is no reason to hide a gift as a sale.
steps.terutzMaskana: He hid it to spare the seller embarrassment.

steps.title: Didn't רב and שמואל already argue about this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that רב and שמואל already argued about this same idea in the case of a man who does קידושין with his own sister.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't they already argue about this once? It was taught: if a man does קידושין with his sister, רב says the money is returned, and שמואל says the money is a gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we need the stolen-land מחלוקת at all, since רב and שמואל already argued about the same idea in a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קידושין cannot take effect between a brother and sister, just as the buyer cannot really get the stolen field. In both cases the man knowingly hands over money for something that will not work. So why does the same מחלוקת show up twice?

keyTerms.meaning: But they already argue about it
One time (already)
One who does קידושין with his sister
The money goes back
The money is a gift

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a contradiction between רב and שמואל. Each one is consistent in both cases. The question is only why the גמרא needs to record the same מחלוקת twice.

phrases.english: But didn't they already disagree about it one time?
phrases.notes: "They" means רב and שמואל, and "it" is the idea from the stolen-land case: money given for something that can't happen.

phrases.english: As it was stated:
One who betroths his sister,
Rav says: The money is returned,
and Shmuel says: The money is a gift.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the whole stolen-land מחלוקת by pointing to an earlier, parallel מחלוקת.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need to record the stolen-land מחלוקת between רב and שמואל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the same principle is already in dispute in the sister case, the second statement looks repetitive.

steps.title: רב's reason: the money to his sister is a deposit
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that the man knows קידושין with his sister will not work, so he must have meant the money as a פקדון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says the money is returned. A person knows that קידושין does not take effect with his sister, so he decided to give it to her as a deposit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רב's reasoning in the sister case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone knows a brother cannot marry his sister. So the money cannot be real קידושין money. רב reads the man's intent as giving it to her for safekeeping, which means he gets it back.

keyTerms.meaning: קידושין takes effect
He made up his mind and gave
As a deposit (for safekeeping)

phrases.english: Rav says: The money is returned,
because a person knows that betrothal does not
take effect with his sister,
and he decided to give it as a deposit.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: מָעוֹת חוֹזְרִין, אָדָם יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֵין קִידּוּשִׁין תּוֹפְסִין בַּאֲחוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Still part of the quoted sister-case source: it gives רב's reasoning. It does not yet answer step 14's question; that answer comes in steps 21–22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The man knew the קידושין would fail, so he meant the money as a פקדון, and it is returned.

steps.title: Why not just call it a deposit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the man didn't tell his sister openly that the money was a deposit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him just tell her it is a deposit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's reading of the man's intent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he really wanted her to hold the money for him, it would be simpler to say so. Using the words of קידושין seems like a strange way to make a deposit.

keyTerms.meaning: So let him say to her

phrases.english: So let him say to her: "as a deposit"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning given for רב in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the money was meant as a deposit.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person who wants to give a deposit would normally say so plainly.

steps.title: She would have refused a deposit
steps.stepSummary: The man thought his sister would not agree to hold a deposit, so he presented the money as קידושין.
steps.simpleTranslation: He thought she would not accept it from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the man used the קידושין wording because he expected her to say no to a plain deposit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding someone else's money is a responsibility, and people often refuse it. So he gave it in a way she would accept. This matches the answer given for the buyer in the stolen-land case (step 10).

keyTerms.meaning: He thought
She would not accept it from him

phrases.english: He thought she would not accept it from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the hidden motive behind the indirect wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If he meant a deposit, he would have said so.
steps.terutzMaskana: He avoided the word 'deposit' because she would have refused to hold it.

steps.title: שמואל's reason: the money to his sister is a gift
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that the man knows קידושין with his sister will not work, so he must have meant the money as a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל says the money is a gift. A person knows that קידושין does not take effect with his sister, so he decided to give it to her as a gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains שמואל's reasoning in the sister case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל starts from the same fact as רב: the man knows the קידושין will fail. But he reads the man's intent differently. He says the man wanted to give her a present, so the money stays with her.

keyTerms.meaning: A person knows
As a gift

phrases.english: And Shmuel says: The money is a gift,
because a person knows that betrothal does not
take effect with his sister,
and he decided to give it as a gift.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רב's reasoning in step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The man knew the קידושין would fail, so he meant the money as a מתנה, and it is not returned.

steps.title: Why not just call it a gift?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the man didn't tell his sister openly that the money was a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him just tell her it is a gift!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's reading the same way it challenged רב's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he really wanted to give her a present, he could have simply said so. Using קידושין wording seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: So let him say to her: 'as a gift'

phrases.english: So let him say to her: "as a gift"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning given for שמואל in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's claim that the money was meant as a gift.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone giving a gift would normally say so plainly.

steps.title: An open gift would embarrass her
steps.stepSummary: Calling it a gift openly would embarrass his sister, so he presented it as קידושין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter is embarrassing to her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the man avoided saying 'gift' so his sister would not feel ashamed to take it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking a handout can feel humiliating, so she might refuse an open gift. Giving it under another name spares her that feeling. This matches the answer given for שמואל in the stolen-land case (step 13).

keyTerms.meaning: It is embarrassing to her
The matter / the thing

phrases.english: The matter is embarrassing to her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the hidden motive behind the indirect wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If he meant a gift, he would have said so.
steps.terutzMaskana: He avoided the word 'gift' to spare her embarrassment.

steps.title: Both cases are needed, part one: רב
steps.stepSummary: If we only had the stolen-land case, we might think רב agrees with שמואל when the money goes to a sister.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both are needed. If it were stated only in this case (stolen land), we would say רב rules there that the money comes back because people do not give gifts to strangers. But with his sister, we might say רב agrees with שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts answering the question from step 14 by showing why the stolen-land case alone would not teach us רב's full view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the stolen-land case the money goes to a stranger, and people don't hand gifts to strangers, so a deposit makes sense. A sister is family, and gifts to family are normal. So without the sister case, we might think רב agrees there that it is a gift.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary (both statements are needed)
For if it were stated only in this case
A stranger / non-relative
I might say he agrees

phrases.english: It is necessary: for if it were stated only in this case,
phrases.notes: "This case" is the buyer of the stolen field.

phrases.english: it is in this case that Rav says so,
because people do not usually
give gifts to a stranger.
But regarding his sister,
I might say he agrees with Shmuel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the question of step 14 and begins the answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: shows each case teaches something the other cannot.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the stolen-land case alone, רב's view might only apply to strangers.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sister case shows that רב says 'deposit' even with a close relative.

steps.title: Both cases are needed, part two: שמואל
steps.stepSummary: If we only had the sister case, we might think שמואל agrees with רב when the money goes to a stranger. So both cases are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it were stated only in that case (his sister), we would say שמואל rules there that it is a gift. But in this case (stolen land), we might say he agrees with רב. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer: the sister case alone would not teach us שמואל's full view, so both cases must be stated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A gift to a sister is natural, so שמואל's 'gift' view fits there easily. With a stranger, one might think even שמואל would say 'deposit.' The stolen-land case shows that שמואל says 'gift' even there.

keyTerms.meaning: In that case

steps.whatToRemember: רב always says money given for a deal that can't work is a deposit and goes back. שמואל always says it is a gift and stays. The two cases are both needed because a stranger and a sister are different: gifts to family are normal, gifts to strangers are not. Each case shows that רב or שמואל holds his view even where it is less expected.

phrases.english: And if it were stated only in that case,
phrases.notes: "That case" is now the sister case.

phrases.english: it is in that case that Shmuel says so;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּהָא אֵימָא מוֹדֶה לֵיהּ לְרַב,
phrases.english: but in this case, I might say he agrees with Rav.
So it is necessary to state both.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אִיתְּמַר בְּהָךְ, בְּהָךְ קָאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the צריכותא begun in step 21 and closes the question from step 14.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both מחלוקות are needed. The stolen-land case shows שמואל's 'gift' view applies even to a stranger. The sister case shows רב's 'deposit' view applies even to a relative.

steps.title: How can the knowing buyer use the land at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how a buyer who knew the land was not the seller's can move onto it and eat its produce, according to both רב and שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whether you follow רב, who says the money is a deposit, or שמואל, who says it is a gift, what right does this buyer have to go onto the land and eat its fruit?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the buyer's behavior. He knew the land was not the seller's, so how can he go onto it and eat its produce?
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב the buyer's money is just a פקדון with the seller. According to שמואל it is a מתנה to the seller. Either way, the buyer did not really buy the land, so his use of it and his eating of its פירות seem to have no basis.

keyTerms.meaning: Both according to... and according to... (the question works for both opinions)
Goes down onto the land, meaning he takes possession of it
With what? On what basis?
Produce or fruit of the land

phrases.english: Both according to Rav, who says it is a deposit,
phrases.notes: This is the money the buyer paid the seller, as in the earlier steps.

phrases.english: and according to Shmuel, who says it is a gift,
this one, on what basis does he go onto the land,
and how does he eat the produce?

steps.triggerLanguage: בין לרב דאמר פקדון בין לשמואל דאמר מתנה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After showing that both cases of the רב and שמואל dispute are needed, the גמרא raises a practical difficulty that applies to both opinions.
steps.kashyaTarget: The behavior of the buyer who knowingly bought land that was not the seller's
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the money is only a deposit or a gift, the buyer never acquired the land, so he seems to have no right to take it over or eat its produce.

steps.title: The buyer plans to act like the seller until the owner comes
steps.stepSummary: The buyer thinks: I will use the land as the seller did, and when the real owner shows up, my money will be a deposit (רב) or a gift (שמואל).
steps.simpleTranslation: He reasons: I will go onto the land, work it and eat from it, just like the seller used to. When the real owner comes, my money will become what it is: a deposit according to רב, or a gift according to שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by explaining the buyer's thinking. He means to use the land the way the seller did, for as long as the real owner stays away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer is not claiming to own the land. He is simply taking the seller's place in using it. Only when the real owner comes and takes the land back does the question of his money come up, and then רב and שמואל each apply their own view.

keyTerms.meaning: He reasons, he thinks to himself
I will go down, I will take possession
The owner of the land
My money (literally, my coins)

phrases.english: He reasons: I will go onto the land
and work it and eat from it

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דַּהֲוָה קָא עָבֵיד אִיהוּ,
phrases.english: just as he used to do,
phrases.notes: "He" is the seller, who was using the land before.

phrases.english: when the owner of the land comes,
my money will be:
according to Rav, who says deposit, a deposit;
according to Shmuel, who says gift, a gift.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the buyer's intention: he steps into the seller's role and is not claiming ownership.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer seems to have no right at all to take over the land and eat its produce.
steps.terutzMaskana: He uses the land the same way the seller did. When the real owner comes, his money is treated as a deposit (רב) or a gift (שמואל).

steps.title: The innocent buyer gets back his money and the value of the improvements
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that a buyer whose land turns out to be stolen gets back both his money and the שבח, even if the seller never spelled out the שבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The הלכה is that the buyer gets his money back and also the value of the improvement, even if the seller did not explicitly promise him the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the final הלכה for the earlier dispute about a buyer who bought land that turned out to be stolen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer gets back the price he paid and also the value of the שבח, the increase in the land's value. This is so even if the seller never wrote or said that he would pay for the שבח. This follows רב's view.

keyTerms.meaning: The final ruling, the הלכה
Money, here the price he paid
Improvement, the increase in the land's value
Spelled out, stated explicitly

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical bottom line for an innocent buyer whose land is taken away by the real owner.

phrases.english: Rava said: The halakha is:

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ לוֹ מָעוֹת וְיֵשׁ לוֹ שֶׁבַח,
phrases.english: he gets the money and he gets the improvement,
phrases.notes: This is the buyer whose land was taken back by the real owner. He collects from the seller.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא פֵּירֵשׁ לוֹ אֶת הַשֶּׁבַח.
phrases.english: even though he did not spell out the improvement for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the analysis, רבא returns to the earlier disputes and rules on them.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An innocent buyer of stolen land collects from the seller both his money and the value of the שבח, even without an explicit promise about the שבח.

steps.title: The knowing buyer gets back his money but not the improvements
steps.stepSummary: רבא continues: if the buyer knew the land was not the seller's, he gets back his money but not the שבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he knew the land was not the seller's and bought it anyway, he gets his money back but not the value of the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his ruling with the case of a buyer who knew from the start that the land was not the seller's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבא rules like רב, who says the money is a פקדון. So the buyer gets his money back. But he took a known risk, so he gets nothing for the שבח.

keyTerms.meaning: He knew about it, he recognized
That it was not his (not the seller's)
And he bought it anyway

steps.whatToRemember: רבא rules like רב in both cases. If the buyer did not know, he gets money and שבח. If he knew, he gets money only, because his money was a פקדון.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with שמואל's view. According to שמואל, a buyer who knew would not get his money back at all, since it was a gift. רבא does not follow that view.

phrases.english: If he knew that it was not his and bought it anyway,

phrases.aramaic: מָעוֹת יֵשׁ לוֹ, שֶׁבַח אֵין לוֹ.
phrases.english: he gets the money; he does not get the improvement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's ruling with the second case, the buyer who knew.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A buyer who knowingly bought land that was not the seller's gets back his money, as a deposit like רב says, but not the שבח.

steps.title: A missing guarantee clause counts as the scribe's mistake
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if the guarantee clause is missing from a document, we treat it as the scribe's mistake, both in loan documents and in sale documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: Leaving out the guarantee is a scribe's mistake, both in loan documents and in documents of buying and selling.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives another final ruling, this time about a document that leaves out the אחריות clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We assume the people meant to include the guarantee and the scribe simply forgot to write it. So the document works as if the guarantee were written in. רבא says this applies to loan documents and to sale documents alike.

keyTerms.meaning: Guarantee, the clause that backs the debt or sale with the person's property
A scribe's mistake
Loan documents
Documents of buying and selling, deeds of sale

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling means a person does not lose his guarantee just because the scribe forgot to write it.

phrases.english: The guarantee is a scribe's mistake,
phrases.notes: He means that when the guarantee is missing from the document, we blame the scribe and treat it as if it were written.

phrases.english: both in loan documents
and in documents of buying and selling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא continues giving final rulings, now on the earlier question about a missing guarantee clause.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A missing אחריות clause is treated as the scribe's mistake, so the guarantee is in force for both loans and sales.

steps.title: שמואל asks: the robber later buys the field from the real owner
steps.stepSummary: שמואל asks רב about a גזלן who sold a stolen field and then bought it from the real owner. Who gets the field?
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל asked רב: If the robber went back and bought the field from the original owners, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. שמואל asks רב what happens when a גזלן who already sold a stolen field later buys that field from its real owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now we dealt with a buyer whose field was taken from him by the real owner. Here the seller himself fixes the problem by buying the field. The question is whether the field now goes to the first buyer, or whether the גזלן may keep it, since he did not own it when he sold it.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (a question put to a teacher or colleague)
He went back and bought it
The original owners, meaning the real owners the field was stolen from
What is the law?

phrases.english: Shmuel asked Rav:
If he went back and bought it from the original owners,
phrases.notes: "He" is the robber who stole the field and already sold it to someone else.

phrases.english: what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רבא's rulings about a buyer of stolen land to a new case where the seller later buys the land himself.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the field go to the first buyer once the גזלן buys it from the real owner, or may the גזלן keep it?

steps.title: רב: the seller sold every right he would ever get
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that the field goes to the buyer, because the seller sold him every right in the field that would ever come into his hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to him: What did the first one sell to the second? Any right that would come into his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers שמואל. The field belongs to the buyer, because the sale covered any right the seller would ever gain in it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We read the sale as broad. It covers what the seller had then, and also any right he gets later. So when the גזלן buys the field from the real owner, that new right passes straight to the לוקח.

keyTerms.meaning: The first one, here the robber who sold the field
The second one, here the buyer
Every right or claim
That will come into his hands

steps.whatToRemember: A seller of a stolen field who later buys it from the real owner cannot take it back. His sale included every right he would ever get in it.

phrases.english: He said to him:
What did the first one sell to the second?
Any right that will come into his hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מָה מָכַר לוֹ רִאשׁוֹן לַשֵּׁנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers שמואל's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The field goes to the buyer, because the original sale included any future rights the seller would gain.

steps.title: Why would the robber want to make the sale good?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב's ruling: why do we assume the seller meant his later rights to go to the buyer?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב's ruling makes sense, and this sets up the next two answers. Why would the seller want the right he bought to pass to his buyer?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a person does not give away something he paid for. The גמרא wants to know what the גזלן gains by buying the field and letting it go to the buyer. Knowing his motive explains why we read the sale so broadly.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רב's answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What motive does the seller have that makes his purchase benefit the buyer?

steps.title: מר זוטרא: he does not want to be called a robber
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא explains that the seller prefers not to have the buyer call him a גזלן.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said: He is pleased not to be called a robber.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא gives the first reason. The seller wants to avoid the buyer calling him a גזלן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the real owner took the field away, the buyer would complain that the seller robbed him. By buying the field and letting it stay with the buyer, the seller avoids that label. The focus is on the buyer, who would be the one calling him a robber.

keyTerms.meaning: It is pleasing to him, meaning he prefers
A robber

phrases.english: Mar Zutra said:
It is pleasing to him that he not be called a robber.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to מאי טעמא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The seller wants to avoid being called a גזלן by the buyer.

steps.title: רב אשי: he wants to stay trustworthy
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the seller wants to keep his reputation as a trustworthy person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: He is pleased to keep his reputation for honesty.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different reason. The seller wants to be known as reliable and honest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב אשי, the issue is not one person's insult but the seller's general good name. He wants people to see him as someone who stands behind his deals.

keyTerms.meaning: To stand in his trustworthiness, meaning to keep his reputation for honesty

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It is pleasing to him to remain in his trustworthiness.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: נִיחָא לֵיהּ דְּלֵיקוּ בְּהֵמָנוּתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second reason, different from מר זוטרא's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The seller wants to keep his reputation as a reliable person.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between the two reasons?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks in what case the reasons of מר זוטרא and רב אשי would lead to different results.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the two reasons ever lead to a different law. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both reasons explain the basic ruling equally well. The גמרא looks for a case where one reason still applies and the other does not.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two reasons just given.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where מר זוטרא's and רב אשי's reasons give different results.

steps.title: The difference: when the buyer has died
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the difference shows up if the לוקח died. It begins to explain the view that the seller only wants to avoid being called a גזלן.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them where the buyer died. According to the one who says he is pleased not to be called a robber —
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the case that separates the two reasons: the buyer has died. It starts to explain מר זוטרא's side, and the sentence continues past the end of this text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under מר זוטרא, the worry is the buyer calling the seller a גזלן. Once the buyer is dead, that worry may be gone. Under רב אשי, the seller's general reputation still matters even after the buyer's death. The full conclusion comes in the next lines.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them
Where the buyer died
The one who says

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence breaks off at the end of this amud. The ruling for each opinion in the case of the dead buyer comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them where the buyer died:
The one who says it is pleasing to him
that he not be called a robber —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers מאי בינייהו by naming the case of a buyer who died.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two reasons differ where the buyer has died. The explanation continues past this text.
